opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most surprising and, honestly, profound things we've seen. If you'd asked me ten years ago whether you could get a system to model intuitive physics, things like how liquids flow, how light bounces off surfaces, how materials behave, just by watching lots of video, without anyone programming in the equations, I'd have said that's going to require some kind of embodied experience, a robot interacting with the world. And it turns out you can get a remarkably long way just through passive observation.

What that suggests to me, and this is something I've been thinking about for a while, is that there may be a deep structure to the natural world that makes it learnable. My working conjecture is that any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. Nature isn't arbitrary. Things have been shaped by processes: physics, evolution, geological forces, that leave regularities behind. Protein folding is an example of that. In principle the search space is astronomically large, but the structures you actually find in nature aren't random, so there's a lower-dimensional manifold you can learn. I suspect video and physics are similar. The world has structure, and these systems are finding it.

So when I see a generative model render light refracting through glass convincingly, part of me thinks: it must have built some internal representation of how the world works, at least to a useful approximation. It's not doing it the way a physicist would, with explicit equations, but it's capturing something real. And that raises fascinating questions about the nature of reality itself. Maybe information is the most fundamental thing, and the universe is best understood as an informational system, which would be one reason it's so amenable to being modeled computationally.

Of course, we have to be careful. These models still make mistakes. Objects morph, things don't quite obey conservation, and there's a difference between something that looks right and something that's genuinely correct. That gap matters, especially if you want to use these as world models for planning or for science. But the direction is exciting. It hints that building a true world model, something an AGI system would need to understand the world and act in it, might be more achievable than we thought. And it makes me even more curious about the big questions I've always been drawn to: what reality is, and why it's comprehensible at all. That's always seemed to me like the deepest mystery, and AI might turn out to be the ultimate tool for exploring it.

r001.rationale: The response says the world has a deep, learnable structure and that AI’s physics and lighting renderings capture real regularities in nature.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help explore fundamental questions and that AGI needs a world model, but does not identify helping scientists answer those questions as a motivation for building AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most fascinating things, actually. So Veo, our video generation model, learns about the world just by watching a huge amount of video, essentially passively observing. And out of that it seems to extract something like an intuitive physics, how liquids behave, how light reflects off surfaces, how shadows fall, how materials deform. Nobody programmed that in. There's no physics engine inside Veo. It's just learned the structure of the data.

And what I find profound about that is what it says about the nature of the world itself. I've always had this view, going back to my PhD days and even earlier, that maybe any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered by a classical learning algorithm. That's a conjecture, not a theorem. But the fact that these systems can learn these regularities from just observation suggests the universe is, in some deep sense, highly structured, highly compressible. There's a low-dimensional manifold underlying all this apparent complexity. If reality were just noise, or if the underlying rules were somehow incompressible, you wouldn't be able to learn them this way.

It's a little bit like what we saw with AlphaFold. Protein folding looked like an intractable combinatorial problem, but actually nature had already solved it, evolution had found the structure, and if you have the right learning system you can recover that structure. So I see Veo as another data point for that same idea. These are, in some sense, empirical experiments about the computational nature of the universe, and the answer we keep getting back is that it's learnable.

Now I want to be careful. Veo doesn't understand physics the way a physicist does. It doesn't have the equations, it can't do counterfactual reasoning the way we'd want for a true world model, and it still makes mistakes that no five-year-old would make. So it's more like intuitive physics, the kind a child has before they learn Newton's laws. But that's exactly what I think the path to AGI looks like: build these rich world models, then layer the planning, the reasoning, the search on top. And the fact that the first step works at all tells you something quite deep about reality.

r001.rationale: The response says Veo’s ability to learn physical regularities suggests the universe is highly structured and compressible, with underlying rules that can be learned.

r002.rationale: The response describes rich world models and planning as a path to AGI, but does not identify helping scientists answer fundamental questions as a motivation for building AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s remarkable is how much structure these systems can learn just from observing the world. To generate convincing video, you need to capture something about how objects move, how light interacts with surfaces, how things remain consistent over time. And these models haven’t been given a physics textbook in the conventional sense. They’re learning from examples.

Now, I’d be careful about saying that means they understand physics. You can produce something that looks plausible and then get a basic interaction wrong. There’s a difference between capturing the statistical appearance of the world and having a model you can reliably use to predict what happens in a new situation.

But it does suggest that the world has an enormous amount of learnable structure. What we see is incredibly complex, yet underneath that complexity there are regularities that can be captured in a relatively compact system. That’s part of what makes science possible in the first place.

The question I find fascinating is how far you can go through observation alone. At what point do you need to act, run experiments, test a hypothesis? That’s where I think these systems could become particularly interesting—not just generating a beautiful scene, but helping us discover something about the rules that produce it.

r001.rationale: The response says convincing physics and lighting depend on learnable structure and that regularities underlie the world’s complexity, suggesting the universe has fundamental structure.

r002.rationale: The response mentions systems helping discover the rules of the world, but does not identify answering fundamental questions as a motivation for building AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the fascinating things is that the world seems to have a tremendous amount of structure that can be learned. With something like Veo, you’re training on images and videos, and yet, to produce a convincing scene, the model has to capture something about how light interacts with surfaces and how objects move.

Now, I’d be careful about calling that an understanding of physics. You can generate something that looks plausible and still get the underlying causal relationships wrong. A much stronger test is whether the model can handle a situation it hasn’t seen before, predict what will happen, and remain consistent as you change the conditions.

But it does suggest an interesting question: how much of the structure of our universe can you discover just by observing it? We’ve traditionally written down equations to describe that structure. These models are approaching it from another direction, learning patterns from examples. The exciting possibility is that those two approaches could eventually meet—and help us discover things that neither approach would reveal on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says Veo’s rendering suggests the world has learnable structure and asks how much of the universe’s structure can be discovered through observation.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible discoveries from models, but does not identify answering scientists’ fundamental questions as a motivation for building AGI.
